en: The Permanent Danger Zone around Mayon Volcano in Albay extends six kilometers from the crater to protect people from lava flows and pyroclastic flows.
Wading in floodwaters after a typhoon can expose you to leptospirosis, a severe bacterial disease spread through the urine of infected rats.
If you feel a strong earthquake near the coast, immediately walk to higher ground because a destructive tsunami wave might follow within minutes.
Emptying stagnant water from old tires and plant pots prevents Aedes aegypti mosquitoes from breeding and spreading the deadly dengue virus.
During the dry El Niño season, drinking plenty of clean water prevents heat exhaustion and dehydration when playing outside under the intense sun.
If caught in a strong rip current at La Union beaches, swim parallel to the shore instead of fighting directly back toward the beach.
Wearing an N95 mask and goggles protects your lungs and eyes from harmful volcanic ashfall when Taal Volcano in Batangas erupts.
Avoid playing near steep mountain slopes in Benguet during heavy rains because saturated soil can easily trigger deadly, fast-moving landslides.
Applying waterproof sunscreen protects your skin from severe sunburns while swimming in the clear, highly reflective waters of the Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park.
Always wear closed shoes when walking in the forests of Mount Makiling to avoid stepping on the venomous Philippine pit viper.
Wearing a long-sleeved rash guard while snorkeling in Palawan protects your skin from the painful stinging tentacles of box jellyfish.
The mountain ranges surrounding Metro Manila can trap vehicle emissions, so wearing a mask helps protect your lungs from harmful daily smog.
